en.title: GTA 6 Cyberleek update: Everything leaked so far, what might be next
en.description: Over the past week or so, someone (or perhaps a group of people) called Cyberleek has been very busy sharing short gameplay clips of Grand Theft Au...
en.fullContent:
Over the past week or so, someone (or perhaps a group of people) called Cyberleek has been very busy sharing short gameplay clips of Grand Theft Auto 6. On Aug. 20, Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of GTA-maker Rockstar Games, filed subpoenas against Microsoft and Discord to try to unmask the leaker, followed soon after by subpoenas against Google and X Corp. Those filings specifically cited "stolen content," seemingly confirming that at least some of the Cyberleek videos are legitimate.

Prior to Thursday's "Extended Look" on Netflix, the GTA 6 leaks represented the first real glimpse of gameplay from the hotly anticipated title. In addition, countless AI-generated videos posing as "leaks" have been circulating widely on social media. So, we've put together a quick list of everything Cyberleek released before seemingly throwing in the towel. We're not going to embed or link to any of these clips; however, they're easy enough to find on X or Reddit if you look hard enough.

At the time of publication, 16 gameplay clips and three map screenshots have been posted by Cyberleek that show different aspects of GTA 6, including glimpses of cutscenes. The leaker did post some minor story spoilers in the most recent release, so be careful if you want to avoid them.

Guess what Apple will release in September in our Big Guessing Game: Apple edition. Enter now for a chance to win an Apple Watch!

Map sneak peek 1: A small, cropped portion of the in-game world map, showing a location called Dalton Island.

Map sneak peek 2: Another cropped portion of the map showing locations called Tequesta Retreat, Gloriana Key, and Catalan Key.

en.title: The Wildest Video Game Budgets Can't Hold A Candle To GTA 6
en.description: The latest Grand Theft Auto is thought to be the most expensive entertainment product ever made.
en.fullContent:
The latest Grand Theft Auto is thought to be the most expensive entertainment product ever made.

When you think about the most expensive entertainment productions ever created, video games are likely not the first thing that comes to mind. Hollywood studios routinely spend hundreds of millions of dollars on a single movie that can have a multi-year production schedule. But video games have actually become just as expensive to produce of late, sometimes even surpassing major films. Case in point: Grand Theft Auto VI looks set to become the most expensive game ever created.

While Rockstar Games hasn't publicly disclosed how much it has spent so far, analysts peg the estimated budget at well over $1 billion, with some putting the current figure at around $1.5 billion. That puts GTA VI in rarefied territory, as it outpaces the known budgets of both major theatrical releases and other AAA games. So what has caused video game development to become so expensive and why is GTA VI's budget in particular eclipsing other big names?

A billion-dollar video game budget may seem surprising at first glance, but it starts to make sense once you consider that a modern game often has just as many moving pieces as a Hollywood production. You need actors, writers, programmers, animators, designers and composers among others to make an expansive open-world game. And short of a few outliers like the Avatar series, movies are typically in active production for a couple of years. GTA VI has been in active development for closer to a decade. Once a game is nearing completion, it usually goes through a rigorous testing process that requires yet another team.

Apart from a handful of indie breakthroughs, it's common for game budgets to quickly spiral into the double or triple-digit millions these days. Game development can also take several years, with hundreds of employees dedicated to a single project.

Development costs and timelines have been steadily rising, though. In 2023, court documents revealed that Sony Interactive Entertainment had spent $212 million on Horizon Forbidden West and $220 million on The Last of Us: Part II.

en.title: Fire destroys 20,000-game collection built over 43 years in Sacramento
en.description: Dave Smith estimates about $500,000 in inventory was inside his longtime Folsom Boulevard Flea Market shop when fire tore through the building Friday
en.fullContent:
Dave Smith estimates about $500,000 in inventory was inside his longtime Folsom Boulevard Flea Market shop when fire tore through the building Friday

Dave Smith estimates about $500,000 in inventory was inside his longtime Folsom Boulevard Flea Market shop when fire tore through the building Friday

A longtime Sacramento video game vendor says a fire at the Folsom Boulevard Flea Market destroyed a collection he spent more than four decades building.

Dave Smith, owner of Dave's Retro Games, said he began selling video games in 1983 after falling in love with Atari. What started small eventually became a full-time business and grew into a collection spanning generations of gaming.

Smith said his store specialized in rare and unusual games and collectibles, with everything from Atari and Nintendo to newer PlayStation titles.

The fire tore through part of the flea market Friday. Smith said a manager called to tell him the building housing his shop was on fire. He arrived minutes later to find flames pouring from the roof.

en.title: First Michigan Retro Game Expo draws big turnout in Kalamazoo
en.description: KALAMAZOO, Mich. — Gamers of all ages gathered in Kalamazoo for the Michigan Retro Game Expo on Saturday.
en.fullContent:
KALAMAZOO, Mich. — Gamers of all ages gathered in Kalamazoo for the Michigan Retro Game Expo on Saturday.

The expo, which organizers said is the first retro game convention to be held in Kalamazoo, took place at the Delta Hotels Kalamazoo Conference Center for a one-day event.

Despite this year being the first year of the expo, organizers couldn't have been happier about the turnout.

"It's a great turnout, this is insane. I didn't know what I expected, but it wasn't a line this far out the door. As of last night, we were just over 700 in presales," said Kris Carlson, CEO of Verge and an organizer of the expo.

The expo offered a myriad of offerings for gamers, including a free play room with classic video games, over 70 art and video game vendors, Dungeons and Dragons sessions, tournaments, and more.

Advertised as an all-ages event, the expo also featured a kids' room with activities geared towards kids. A representative from Nintendo was also at the expo.
